26.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about 'State' under Article 12?

xa: **Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967)**: statutory bodies are "**other authorities**".
**Ajay Hasia (1981)**: the test is **how it was created and controlled**, not the form.
Writs do not ordinarily lie against **private bodies**, unless the State acts in collusion.

26.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib?

26.s: A private organisation performs a public activity, but no governmental authority is shown to be involved in the alleged violation. Which position is most consistent with the general rule concerning writs?
o: A writ can never lie against a private organisation under any circumstances
A writ ordinarily lies because every public activity makes the organisation ‘State’
A writ does not ordinarily lie merely because the organisation performs a public activity
A writ lies only when Parliament specifically authorises the organisation
26.x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely on the basis of their public activity. The rule is not absolute, since State collusion can alter the position.
26.tq: Apply the ordinary rule while avoiding the absolute trap in the words ‘every’ and ‘never’.
xs: Writs do **not ordinarily lie against private bodies** merely for a public activity — option **(3)**.
The rule is not absolute: a writ may lie if the **State acts in collusion** — so option (1) is too wide.
xa: If **Arts. 19/21** are violated **by a private individual**, the remedy is an **ordinary legal remedy, not a writ**.
"State" under **Art. 12** includes **other authorities** in India or under GoI control.
A body is "State" if **dominated** by govt (**Pradeep Kumar Biswas, 2002**).

26.s: In Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002), on what basis was a body held to be 'State'?

26.s: According to Article ______ the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges the Fundamental rights
26.x: Art. 13(2): the State shall not make any law that takes away or abridges FRs; such a law is void to that extent.

26.s: X was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term 'law' as provided under Article 13, Part III of the Constitution of India. X explained that the meaning of the term 'law' in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. Y pointed out that the term 'law' in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which 'X' was not convinced. Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below:
o: X is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom.
The view of Y that 'law' included custom is not correct.
The views of both 'X' and 'Y' are correct.
The view of only Y is correct.
26.x: Art. 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification and custom or usage having the force of law. X's denial that custom is included contradicts the text, so only Y's view is correct.

26.s: Which Article of the Constitution gives precedence to Constitutional provisions over the laws made by the Union Parliament/State Legislatures?
26.x: Article 13 voids laws of Parliament and State legislatures inconsistent with the Fundamental Rights, giving constitutional (Part III) provisions precedence; Art. 245 is the extent of laws, 32 remedies, 326 adult suffrage.

26.s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court
Only an Act passed by Parliament
26.x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
26.tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
xs: Under **Art. 13(3)**, "law" includes **ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage** — option **(1)**.
Amendments under **Art. 368** are excluded by **Art. 13(4)** (**24th Amendment 1971**) — option (2) wrong.
xa: **13(1):** pre-constitution laws inconsistent with FRs are **void** to that extent.
**13(2):** the State shall not make a law **abridging FRs**.
**Art. 13** makes FRs **supreme over ordinary law**.

26.s: How are constitutional amendments made under Article 368 treated under Article 13(4)?
o: Treated as ordinary laws under Article 13
Void if they abridge any Fundamental Right
26.x: Article 13(4), inserted by the 24th Amendment, says Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368.
xa: The 24th Amendment answered **Golaknath (1967)**, which gave FRs a **transcendental** position.
**Golaknath** is also the case for **prospective overruling**.
FRs can be limited only by a **constitutional amendment**, not ordinary law.

26.s: Article 13(1) makes void, to the extent of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights, laws in force before which event?
26.x: Article 13(1) covers laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution, not 'before Independence'.

26.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that Fundamental Rights occupy a transcendental position and that Parliament cannot abridge them, a position later countered by the 24th Amendment (1971)?
26.x: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a transcendental position and held Parliament could not abridge them; the 24th Amendment (1971) responded by adding Art. 13(4). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) came after and laid down the basic structure; Shankari Prasad had upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21.
xs: **Golaknath (1967)** gave FRs a **transcendental** position — Parliament **cannot** abridge them — option **(2)**.
The **24th Amendment (1971)** countered it by adding **Art. 13(4)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** came later and set the **basic structure** limit; **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** widened **Art. 21**.
xa: **Golaknath** also applied **prospective overruling** — the ruling operates only for the future.
⚠ **1967** twice: **Golaknath** (Art. 13) and **Rajasthan SEB** (Art. 12).
Limiting FRs now needs a **constitutional amendment**, subject to the **basic structure**.

26.s: In which case did the Supreme Court first hold that a constitutional amendment is not 'law' under Article 13?
26.x: Shankari Prasad (1951) held an amendment is not 'law'; Golaknath (1967) took the opposite view.

26.s: Which Amendment added Article 13(4)?
26.x: The 24th Amendment (1971) added Article 13(4) in reply to Golaknath.

26.s: A law is void only to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights and if that part is severable, the law remains valid and alive which is consistent with fundamental rights. This doctrine is
26.x: Severability: a law is void only to the extent of inconsistency; the severable consistent part remains valid.

26.s: The doctrine of ______ envisages that a pre constitutional law inconsistent with a fundamental right are not wiped out totally from the statute book after the commencement of the constitution
26.x: Doctrine of eclipse: an inconsistent pre-constitution law is not wiped out but dormant, and revives when the conflict is removed (Bhikaji Narain, 1955).

26.s: Which case is associated with the widening of Article 21 through progressive interpretation?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
26.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened the interpretation of Article 21 and is an important example of progressive constitutional interpretation.
26.tq: Link the interpretive doctrine with its constitutional example.
xs: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** widened **Art. 21** — option **(1)**.
**Basheshar Nath** = **waiver**; **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras** = **eclipse** — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: **Progressive interpretation** treats the Constitution as a **living document**.
**Trauma care** was read into Art. 21 in **SaveLIFE Foundation v. UoI (2026)**.
Courts have also read **shelter** into **Art. 21**.

26.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of absolute liability for hazardous industries?
o: Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh
M.C. Mehta, Oleum gas leak case
26.x: The absolute liability principle was evolved in M.C. Mehta’s 1987 Oleum gas leak case. It imposes liability on hazardous industries without the exceptions available under strict liability.
26.tq: Distinguish absolute liability from public trust and severability by the underlying subject.
xs: **Absolute liability** comes from **M.C. Mehta (1987)** — the **Oleum gas leak** case — option **(4)**.
A **hazardous industry** is liable without the exceptions of **strict liability**.
**Golaknath** = prospective overruling; **Motor General Traders** = severability (some notes).
xa: **Progressive interpretation**: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**.
**Waiver**: **Basheshar Nath v CIT (1959)**.
**Eclipse**: **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)**.

26.s: Which doctrine is most directly applicable when a law enacted by one legislature appears to encroach upon a subject in another legislative List?
26.x: Pith and substance is the relevant doctrine for examining Union-State List encroachment by looking at the true nature and character of the law.
26.tq: Identify the doctrine from the federal legislative competence scenario.
xs: **Pith and substance** is the doctrine for **Union-State List encroachment** — option **(4)**.
Its variant is the **aspect doctrine**.
**Prospective overruling** and **absolute liability** are not federal doctrines.
xa: Other federal doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **territorial nexus**, incidental and ancillary powers, **repugnancy**.
**Territorial nexus**: a state law is valid outside the State if sufficient connection (**R.M.D.C., 1957**).
Exam angle: **doctrine-to-case matching**.

26.s: Which of the following pairs of doctrine and meaning is wrongly matched?
o: Eclipse – Only the inconsistent portion of a law is void
Waiver – A person cannot give up a Fundamental Right
Prospective overruling – Ruling operates only for the future
Severability – Only the inconsistent portion of a law is void
26.x: Eclipse means an inconsistent law stays dormant and may revive; voiding only the inconsistent portion is severability.
xa: Cases: eclipse — **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)**; severability — **A.K. Gopalan (1950)**, **R.M.D.C. (1957)**.
Waiver — **Basheshar Nath (1959)**; prospective overruling — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Territorial nexus**: state law valid outside the State if sufficient connection (**R.M.D.C., 1957**).

26.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Severability — State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills
26.x: State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is associated with the extension of the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws affecting non-citizens. Severability is associated with cases such as A.K. Gopalan, R.M.D.C. and Motor General Traders.
26.tq: Find the wrongly assigned case rather than recalling the doctrine alone.
xs: The wrong pair is **Severability — State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills** — option **(4)**.
**Ambica Mills (1974)** is an **eclipse** case: a post-constitution law stays valid for **non-citizens**.
The others are right: **Waiver** — Basheshar Nath; **Prospective overruling** — Golaknath; **Eclipse** — Bhikaji Narain Dhakras.
xa: Severability cases: **A.K. Gopalan (1950)**, **R.M.D.C. (1957)**; some notes cite **Motor General Traders (1984)**.
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (**1955**): the law revived after the **1st Amendment**.
⚠ Eclipse is mainly for **pre-constitution** laws.

26.s: Under the doctrine of eclipse, what happens to a law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights?
o: Is void from the beginning and can never revive
Becomes dormant and revives when the conflict is removed
Remains valid except for the inconsistent part
Can be waived by the affected citizen
26.x: Under eclipse the law is dormant, not dead, and revives when the conflict is removed.

26.s: The doctrine of eclipse was applied in which case?
o: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
26.x: In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955) the law revived after the 1st Amendment; Basheshar Nath is the waiver case.

26.s: What did the Supreme Court hold in Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959)?
o: Only the inconsistent part of a law is void
A pre-constitution law revives after amendment
A person cannot waive a Fundamental Right
Rulings operate only for the future

26.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling is associated with which case?
26.x: Golaknath (1967) applied prospective overruling; 1967 is also the year of Rajasthan SEB, an Article 12 case.

26.s: In which case was the doctrine of eclipse extended to post-constitution laws in respect of non-citizens?
o: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP

26.s: Under which doctrine can a State law operate outside the State if there is a sufficient connection, as held in State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957)?

26.s: In which of the following cases was the doctrine of severability applied?

26.s: Right to vote and to be elected in India is a
26.x:

Article 48 provides for the organisation of agriculture. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48 provides for the organisation of animal husbandry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 48A provides for safeguarding forests and wildlife. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 49 provides for the protection of monuments of national importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 49 provides for the protection of places of national importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xa: The **86th Amendment (2002)** changed **Art. 45** to **early childhood care and education** below **6 years**.
Education for **6-14** is now an FR under **Art. 21A**.
**Art. 50** = **separation of the Judiciary from the Executive**.

31.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections — Article 46
31.x: C is correct: Article 46 protects the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections. The others are mismatched: village panchayats are Art. 40 (not 43), cottage industries are Art. 43 (not 40), and prohibition of intoxicating drinks is Art. 47 (not 48).
31.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pair and eliminate the shifted numbers.
xs: **Art. 46** — interests of **SCs, STs and weaker sections** — option **(3)**.
Protection of weaker sections is a DPSP only — **not an FD**.
xa: DPSP **Art. 48A** = State to protect the environment; **Art. 49** = **monuments**.
FD look-alikes: environment **51A(g)**, composite culture **51A(f)**.

31.s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with a social order based on social, economic and political justice and the minimisation of inequalities?
31.x: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.
31.tq: Distinguish the general welfare-and-inequality provision from the specific objectives listed in Article 39.
xs: **Article 38**: social order of **social, economic, political justice** and **minimising inequalities** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 39** is livelihood, resources, equal pay; **Art. 41** is right to work; **Art. 46** is SC/ST/weaker sections.
xa: **38(2)** (minimise inequalities) was added by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
Art. 38 is grouped as a **Socialist** principle.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly states the subject matter of Articles 39(b) and 39(c)?
o: 39(b): distribution of community resources for the common good; 39(c): prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production
39(b): protection of monuments; 39(c): promotion of international peace
39(b): right to work; 39(c): free legal aid
31.x: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.
31.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring Directive Principles by their exact constitutional wording.
xs: **39(b)**: **material resources** distributed for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth** and means of production — option **(1)**.
APPSC G2 **2025**: both statements are in the Constitution.
xa: Implemented by **land reforms**, **zamindari abolition**, **ceiling laws**.
**Monuments** = **Art. 49**; **international peace** = **Art. 51**; **equal pay** = **39(d)**.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly matches the constitutional provision with its nature?
o: Article 24 — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 39(f) — Directive Principle of State Policy
Article 21A — Directive Principle of State Policy
31.x: Article 39(f) is a Directive Principle of State Policy. Articles 24 and 21A are Fundamental Rights, while Article 39(e) is also a Directive Principle.
31.tq: Use the Fundamental Right–DPSP distinction to eliminate swapped classifications.
xs: **Art. 39(f)** is a **Directive Principle of State Policy** — option **(3)**.
**39(e)** is also a DPSP, not a Fundamental Right — option (2) wrong.
**Art. 21A** (education 6-14) is a **Fundamental Right** — option (4) wrong.
xa: 39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**Art. 21A** came with the **86th Amendment (2002)**.

31.s: After the constitutional changes relating to education, what does Article 45 direct the State to provide?
o: Free legal aid to all citizens
Early childhood care and education until six years of age
Free and compulsory education from six to fourteen years
31.x: Article 45 now covers early childhood care and education until six; education from six to fourteen is the Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

31.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief?
31.x: Article 42 covers humane conditions of work and maternity relief; 38 is welfare of the people, 39 livelihood and equal pay, 41 right to work.
n: Article 38 directs the State to promote the welfare of the people. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for adequate means of livelihood. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for equal pay for equal work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for the protection of children. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for the right to work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for the right to education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for public assistance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 42 provides for just and humane conditions of work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 42 provides for maternity relief. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xa: **39A** = **equal justice** and **free legal aid** (42nd Amendment).
**Art. 43** = **living wage** and **cottage industries**.
**Art. 41** was given effect through **MGNREGA (2005)**.

31.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 43 provides for a living wage and a decent standard of life.
Article 47 directs the State to raise the level of nutrition, raise the standard of living and improve public health.
Article 43A directs the State to provide for the participation of workers in the management of agriculture.
Article 43A provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries.
31.x: C is incorrect: Article 43A provides for workers' participation in the management of industries, not agriculture. Articles 43 (living wage) and 47 (nutrition, public health) are stated correctly.
31.tq: Watch for one word changed in a provision.
n: Article 43 provides for a living wage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 43 provides for a decent standard of life. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 43A provides for the participation of workers in the management of industries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]

Article 47 directs the State to raise the standard of living. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 47 directs the State to improve public health. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: The incorrect statement is that Article 43A provides workers' participation in **management of agriculture** — option **(3)**.
**Article 43A** provides **workers' participation in management** of **industries**, added by the **42nd Amendment**.
**Art. 43** (**living wage**, decent standard of life) and **Art. 47** (**nutrition**, **public health**) are stated correctly.
xa: **Art. 48** covers organisation of **agriculture** and **animal husbandry** on scientific lines.
**Art. 47** also directs **prohibition** of **intoxicating drinks and drugs**.
**Art. 43B** (**co-operative societies**) came with the **97th Amendment**.

31.s: Which of the following Directive Principles is grouped under the Gandhian, not the Socialist, principles?
31.x: Article 43B (co-operative societies) is Gandhian; Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under Socialist principles.
xa: Liberal-intellectual: **44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51**.

31.s: Which of the following was NOT added to the Directive Principles by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
o: Article 39A – Equal justice and free legal aid
31.x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; the 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A, 48A and 39(f).
xa: The 42nd also added **39(f)** (children's development).
**43B** came by the **97th (2011)**; Art. 45 substituted by the **86th (2002)**.

31.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Article 40 deals with the organisation of Village Panchayats.
Article 50 deals with the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive.
Article 43B was added by the 42nd Amendment.
Article 46 promotes the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections.
31.x: C is incorrect: Article 43B (co-operative societies) was added by the 97th Amendment (2011), not the 42nd. The others are right: Article 40 panchayats, 50 separation of judiciary, 46 weaker sections.
31.tq: Check which amendment added each 'A/B' Article.
n: Article 40 concerns the organisation of Village Panchayats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 46 concerns the promotion of the interests of Scheduled Castes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 46 concerns the promotion of the interests of Scheduled Tribes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 46 concerns the promotion of weaker sections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 50 provides for the separation of the Judiciary from the Executive. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Article 43B was added by the 42nd Amendment** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 43B** (**co-operative societies**) was added by the **97th Amendment (2011)**.
**Art. 40** (**village panchayats**), **Art. 50** (**separation of judiciary**), **Art. 46** (**weaker sections**) are correct.
xa: Order to remember: **42nd → 44th → 86th → 97th**.
The **44th (1978)** added **38(2)**; the **86th (2002)** substituted **Art. 45**.

31.s: Environmental protection is provided under which provision as a Fundamental Duty?
31.x: Protecting the environment is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g). Article 48A makes it a Directive Principle, not a duty.
31.tq: Separate the duty (51A(g)) from the directive (48A).
n: Environmental protection is provided under Article 51A(g) as a Fundamental Duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: Environmental protection as a Fundamental Duty is **Article 51A(g)** — option **(4)**.
**Art. 48A** is the **Directive Principle** on environment, not a duty.
**Art. 45** = **early childhood care and education**; **Art. 49** = **monuments**.
xa: Both **48A** and **51A(g)** came with the **42nd Amendment**.
**51A(g)** covers **forests, lakes, rivers and wild life** and **compassion for living creatures**.
**48A** is in the **Liberal-Intellectual** group.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT a Directive Principle of State Policy?
31.x: The Right to Information is a legal right under the RTI Act, 2005; right to work (41), UCC (44) and maternity relief (42) are DPSPs.

31.s: Article 43A provides for participation of workers in the management of which of the following?
31.x: Article 43A, added by the 42nd Amendment, concerns workers' participation in the management of industries, not agriculture.

31.s: Which of the following is a Directive Principle and NOT a Fundamental Right under the Constitution?
o: Right to education for children aged 6-14
31.x: The right to work is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for 6-14 (Art. 21A), forced labour ban (Art. 23) and equality (Art. 14) are Fundamental Rights.

31.s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to secure the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement?
31.x: Article 41 deals with the right to work, to education and to public assistance.

31.s: Which Article of the Directive Principles directs the State to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health?
31.x: Article 47 covers nutrition, public health and prohibition of intoxicating drinks and injurious drugs.

31.s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to protect monuments and places of national importance?
31.x: Article 49, a Directive Principle, provides for the protection of monuments and places of national importance.

31.s: Which is the last Article of Part IV of the Constitution, dealing with the promotion of international peace and security?
31.x: Article 51, the last Article of Part IV, deals with international peace and security and respect for international law.

31.s: Article 48 directs the State to ban the slaughter of cows and calves. Under which entry does the power to legislate on this subject lie?
31.x: Article 48 is only a directive; the power to legislate on cow slaughter lies with the States under State List Entry 15 (livestock).

31.s: If Education is the result of social change it means that social change has created a demand for:
31.src: APPSC Hostel Welfare Officer Grade-II (Male & Female) in AP
31.x: If education is a result (dependent variable) of social change, then the change has created a demand for education, i.e. new knowledge and skills that the school must supply (printed key: Conscience, which does not follow from the stem).

31.s: State to direct its policy towards securing for men and women equally the right to an adequate means of livelihood is mentioned in the Constitution of India under
31.src: APPSC Group-III Mains Panchayat Secretary (Grade-IV) Paper-I
31.x: Art. 39(a), adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally, is a Directive Principle of State Policy.

31.s: Which one of the following is included in the Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
Protection of life and personal liberty
Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
31.x: Equal pay for equal work (39(d)) is a DPSP; conviction protection (20), life and liberty (21) and minority interests (29) are FRs.

31.s: Identify the correct pair mentioning the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India-
o: Equal justice and free legal aid – Article 42
Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry –
That there is equal pay for equal work for both men
31.x: Only equal pay – Art. 39(d) is right; free legal aid is 39A, agriculture is 48 and village panchayats 40.

31.s: What does Article 39(a) of the Constitution direct the State to secure?
o: The right to work in every circumstance
Free legal aid to economically weaker citizens
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally
31.x: Article 39(a) directs the State to secure adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally. Equal pay for equal work is contained in Article 39(d).
31.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring clauses of the same Article.
xs: **39(a)**: **adequate means of livelihood** for men and women **equally** — option **(4)**.
**Equal pay** is **39(d)**; **free legal aid** is **39A**; **right to work** is **Art. 41**.
xa: **39(b)**: material resources for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth**.
Dignity of women links **39(a), (d), (e), 42** with FD **51A(e)**.

31.s: Which clause of Article 39 protects children against exploitation and abandonment and provides for their development in freedom and dignity?
31.x: Article 39(f) directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment. The present wording was introduced through the 42nd Amendment.
31.tq: Identify the exact sub-clause by its distinctive subject matter.
xs: **Article 39(f)**: children to develop in **freedom and dignity**, protected from **exploitation** and **moral/material abandonment** — option **(4)**.
39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**39(d)** = equal pay; **39(e)** = health of workers and children; **39(c)** = concentration of wealth.
xa: The 42nd also added **39A, 43A, 48A**.
Education of children: **Art. 45** (below 6), FR **21A**, FD **51A(k)**.

31.s: Which clause of Article 39 provides for equal pay for equal work for both men and women?
31.x: Article 39(d) deals with equal pay; 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and children from unsuited work.
xa: 39(e) also protects the **tender age of children** from abuse.
**39(f)**: children's development in freedom and dignity.

31.s: Which clause of Article 39 directs that the tender age of children and the health of workers are not abused?
31.x: Article 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and the tender age of children; 39(d) is equal pay for equal work.

31.s:
Which of the following Directive Principles do not follow Gandhian Principles?
1) Organization of Village Panchayats
2) Common Civil Code
3) Promotion of cottage Industry in rural areas
4) Right to work
31.x: UCC (liberal-intellectual) and right to work (socialist) are not Gandhian; village panchayats and cottage industries are.

31.s: The Directive principles of State Policy may be classified in to which of the following parts for the sake of convenient study?
31.x: For study, DPSPs are grouped as socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual; the Constitution itself does not classify them.

31.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of Articles generally classified as Gandhian principles?
31.x: Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are generally included among Gandhian principles. The other sets contain Socialist or Liberal-intellectual principles.
31.tq: Classify by the group as a whole and eliminate mixed sets.
xs: **Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46** are all **Gandhian** — option **(1)**.
**44, 45, 48A, 50** and **49, 50, 51** are **Liberal-intellectual**; **38, 39, 41, 42** are **Socialist**.
xa: 40 = panchayats; 43 = **cottage industries**; 43B = co-operatives; 46 = **SC/ST/weaker sections**.
47 (prohibition) and 48 (cow slaughter) are also Gandhian.

31.s: Which of the following is true of the classification of Directive Principles into Socialist, Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual groups?
o: An academic arrangement used for study
Made by the Supreme Court in Part IV
31.x: The Constitution does not itself classify the Directive Principles; the three-fold grouping is an academic arrangement.

31.s: How many Articles are counted in the Gandhian group of Directive Principles?
31.x: The Gandhian group has six Articles: 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47 and 48.

31.s: Article 43B (co-operative societies) falls under which group of Directive Principles?
31.x: Article 43B is a Gandhian principle; Articles 38, 39A and 47 are in the Socialistic group.

31.s:
With regards to Directive Principles of State Policy, what is the correct chronological order in which the following additions/changes were incorporated into the Constitution of India through amendments?

I. The adding of a second aspect relating to Article 38.

II. The changing of the subject-matter of Article 45.

III. The adding of Article 43B.

IV. The adding of Article 48A.
31.x: 48A (42nd, 1976) → second clause of Art. 38 (44th, 1978) → Art. 45 changed (86th, 2002) → 43B (97th, 2011): IV, I, II, III.

31.s: Which article of Indian Constitution ensures Early Childhood Care and Education to children below the age of 6 years?
31.src: APPSC Technical Assistants (Hydrology) in AP Ground Water Su
31.x: Article 45 (as substituted in 2002) provides early childhood care and education for children below six.

31.s: How many directive principles were added to Part-IV of the constitution by the 42nd Amendment?
31.x:
Most books and keys: four (39(f), 39A, 43A, 48A). Strictly: three new Articles (39A, 43A, 48A) were inserted and 39(f) recast (Rocket Polity p.46; PMF Polity p.81).
The 42nd Amendment added four DPSPs: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.

31.s: In Which year it was inserted in the Constitution of India that the State shall secure free legal aid to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities?
31.x: Art. 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) came with the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (in force 3 Jan 1977).

31.s: Which of the following Directive Principles of State Policy was added to the Constitution at a later date?
31.x: Free legal aid (39A) was added in 1976; panchayats, cow protection and UCC were original.

31.s: Which of the following Article was inserted by the 42nd Constitution Amendment to provide for participation of workers in management?
31.x: Art. 43A, workers in management, was inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

31.s: Which principle among the following was added to the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution?
o: Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
Participation of workers in the management of
Right to work, education and public assistance
Securing living wage and human conditions of work
31.x: The 42nd added Art. 43A (workers in management); equal pay, right to work and living wage were original.

31.s: Which of the following was not added to the Directive Principles by the 42nd Amendment of the Constitution?
o: Protection of Children and youth from exploitation
Equal justice and free legal aid
Participation of workers in the management of
31.x: The Uniform Civil Code (Art. 44) was in the original Constitution; 39(f) children, 39A free legal aid and 43A workers in management were added by the 42nd Amendment.

31.s: By which Amendment was the Ninth Schedule added to the Constitution?
31.x: The First Amendment, 1951 introduced the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B; the 73rd Amendment dealt with Panchayati Raj.
xa: Land reforms implement **39(b), (c)**: zamindari abolition, ceiling laws.
The 73rd gave panchayats **constitutional status** under **Art. 40**.

31.s:
Arrange the following changes to the Directive Principles in chronological order:
A. Insertion of Article 43B (co-operative societies)
B. Substitution of Article 45 (early childhood care and education)
C. Insertion of Articles 39A, 43A and 48A
D. Insertion of Article 38(2) (minimising inequalities)
31.x: 42nd Amendment (1976) added 39A, 43A, 48A; 44th (1978) added 38(2); 86th (2002) substituted Article 45; 97th (2011) added Article 43B.
xa: APPSC **2024** asked two chronology questions on these four.
The 42nd also added **39(f)**.

31.s: By which Amendment was Article 38(2) added to the Directive Principles?
31.x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; Article 43B came by the 97th (2011) and the present Article 45 by the 86th (2002).
xa: 86th also linked to **Art. 21A** and **51A(k)**.

31.s: Article 43B on co-operative societies was added by which Amendment?
31.x: The 97th Amendment, 2011 added Article 43B, the last DPSP added.

31.s:
Consider the following statements about amendments to the Directive Principles:
1. The 44th Amendment added Article 38(2).
2. The 86th Amendment substituted Article 45.
3. The 42nd Amendment added Article 44.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
31.x: The 44th added 38(2) and the 86th substituted Article 45; the UCC (Article 44) was not added by the 42nd Amendment.

31.s: On which date did Article 39A on free legal aid come into force?
31.x: Article 39A was added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment and came into force on 3 January 1977; 9 November 1995 is when the Legal Services Authorities Act came into force.

31.s: Who said the Directive principles are 'a post-dated cheque'?
31.x: K.T. Shah compared the Directives to a cheque on a bank payable at the bank's convenience, quoted in quiz books as a 'post-dated cheque'. Gandhi, not Shah, called the Cripps offer a 'post-dated cheque', and Nehru added 'on a crashing bank'.

31.s: Who considers the Directive Principles of State Policy to be "aimed at furthering the goals of the social revolution...."?
31.x: Granville Austin wrote that the Directive Principles (with the FRs) aim at furthering the goals of the social revolution, and he called them the 'conscience of the Constitution'. Ambedkar called them a 'novel feature'.

31.s: “The Directive Principles of State Policy is a cheque which is paid on Bank’s Convenience," Who said it?
31.x: K.T. Shah called the Directives a cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank; Ambedkar called them a 'novel feature'.

31.s: Which of the following descriptions of the Directive Principles is an approving one, not a criticism?
o: No better than New Year's resolutions
A novel feature of the Indian Constitution
31.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution; the other remarks criticise their non-justiciable character.
xa: **K.T. Shah**: a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
**K.C. Wheare**: a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**.
**Granville Austin**: FRs and DPSPs together are the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Art. 37**: Part IV **shall not be enforceable by any court**, yet the principles are **fundamental in the governance of the country**.

31.s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'a manifesto of aims and aspirations'?
31.x: K.C. Wheare called them a manifesto of aims and aspirations; Ivor Jennings called them 'pious aspirations' and T.T. Krishnamachari 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'.
xa: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called DPSPs a "**novel feature**" — the approving remark.
**Nasiruddin**: "no better than **New Year's resolutions**" broken on the second of January.
**Granville Austin**: FRs and DPSPs together are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".
**K.T. Shah** also wanted the **right to work** as an FR.

31.s: The debate over the right to work as a Fundamental Right versus a Directive Principle was associated in the Constituent Assembly with which pair?
o: K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar
Rajendra Prasad and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
N. Rau and K. M. Munshi
31.x: The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar.
31.tq: Match the constitutional debate with the specific participants named in it.
xs: The right-to-work debate (FR vs DPSP) in the Constituent Assembly was between **K.T. Shah** and **B.R. Ambedkar** — option **(1)**.
**K.T. Shah** wanted the **right to work** as an FR; it stayed a directive under **Art. 41**.
K.T. Shah also called the DPSPs a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
xa: **Art. 41**: right to **work**, education, public assistance (unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement).
**MGNREGA (2005)** made the right to work a legal right; since replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.
The fall in rural work under the **VB-GRAM G Act** revived the right-to-work debate (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ Ambedkar called the DPSPs a **novel feature**; Shah's remark was critical.

31.s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'?
31.x: 'Dustbin of sentiments' was T.T. Krishnamachari's phrase; Granville Austin called FRs and DPSPs the conscience of the Constitution.

31.s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'pious aspirations'?
31.x: Ivor Jennings called them pious aspirations; K.T. Shah compared them to a cheque payable at the bank's convenience.

31.s: Who called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution?
31.x: Ambedkar's 'novel feature' is the only approving remark; K.C. Wheare called them a manifesto of aims and aspirations.

31.s: Who said that the Directive Principles were 'no better than New Year's resolutions' which are broken on the second of January?
31.x: Nasiruddin compared the DPSPs to New Year's resolutions broken on the second of January.

31.s: Who described the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles together as the 'conscience of the Constitution'?
31.x: Granville Austin called the FRs and DPSPs together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

31.s: Which Article of Indian constitution provides provisions of Right to free Legal service of accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal service?
31.x: Art. 39A (42nd Amendment) directs the State to secure equal justice and free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities. Art. 43 is the living wage, and there is no Art. 46A.

31.s:
Consider the following pairs: Provision in the Constitution of India Stated under
1. Separation of Judiciary from the Executive in the public services of the State The Directive Principles of the State Policy
2. Valuing and preserving the rich heritage of our composite culture The Fundamental Duties

31.x: All three pairs are correct: separation of judiciary is Art. 50 (DPSP), the composite culture is FD 51A(f), and the ban on child labour below 14 in factories is FR Art. 24.

32.tq: Apply the constitutional consequence separately to an enforceable right and a non-justiciable directive.
xs: A law violating an FR may be **void under Article 13**, but a law **cannot be struck down** merely for violating a DPSP — option **(1)**.
DPSPs are **non-justiciable** under **Art. 37**, so (2) is wrong: Art. 37 does not make laws void.
(3) and (4) are wrong: only FR-violating laws are void; such laws are open to **judicial review**.
xa: FRs are mostly **negative** obligations; DPSPs **positive** directions to the State.
FRs aim at **political democracy**; DPSPs at **social and economic democracy**.
**Harmonious construction**: read Part III and Part IV **together** so both operate (**Kerala Education Bill, 1958**; **Minerva Mills, 1980**).

36.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?

xa: Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**.

Ministers may publicly oppose Cabinet decisions
Only Cabinet Ministers share responsibility for policy
40.x: Collective responsibility requires all ministers to support Cabinet decisions publicly; a minister unwilling to defend such a decision must resign.

40.s: In which House can a no-confidence motion against the Union Council of Ministers be moved?
o: a joint sitting of both Houses
40.x: Under Article 75(3) the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, so a no-confidence motion lies only there; even Rajya Sabha ministers are responsible to the Lok Sabha.

40.s: What is the result of the death or resignation of the Prime Minister?
o: The Council of Ministers going out of office
Automatic dissolution of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most minister automatically becoming Prime Minister
Only the Prime Minister's office falling vacant
40.x: The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, so his death or resignation means the Council of Ministers as a whole goes out of office.
xa: **Loss of LS confidence** (no-confidence motion, defeat on a money bill/major policy) → **whole ministry resigns**.
Defeat in the **Rajya Sabha** does **not** bring down the government.

40.s: Who administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers?
40.x: The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers in accordance with the Third Schedule.
40.tq: Identify the constitutional authority associated with administering the oath.
xs: Oaths of **office and secrecy** to Union Ministers are administered by the **President** (**Third Schedule**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **PM**, **CJI** or **Speaker** play no part in ministers' oaths.
xa: The **oath of secrecy** ensures the **secrecy** of Cabinet deliberations.
Ministers hold office at the **President's pleasure** (**Art. 75(2)**).
**Arts. 74-75** create the Council of Ministers.

40.s: Which Article in the States corresponds to Article 75(3) on collective responsibility?
40.x: Article 164(2) provides that the Council of Ministers in a State is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
40.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring constitutional provisions by matching the subject with the exact Article.
xs: The State counterpart of **Art 75(3)** is **Article 164(2)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under it the State CoM is collectively responsible to the **Legislative Assembly**.
xa: **Art 75(3):** Union CoM collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.
⚠ **75(3)** = collective; **75(2)** = individual responsibility.
A **no-confidence motion** at the Union lies **only in the Lok Sabha**.

40.s: Which of the following does NOT, by itself, require the whole Union ministry to resign?
o: Passage of a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha
Defeat on a money bill in the Lok Sabha
Defeat on a major policy measure in the Lok Sabha
Defeat of the Government in the Rajya Sabha
40.x: Only loss of Lok Sabha confidence can lead the ministry to resign; defeat in the Rajya Sabha does not by itself compel resignation.
xa: The no-confidence motion lies **only in the Lok Sabha**.
**PM's death/resignation** dissolves the Council.
RS ministers are also responsible to the **Lok Sabha**.

40.x: Under Article 75(2), ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. The PM may advise dismissal in practice, but constitutionally it is the President.

40.x: Article 75(2) provides that a Union Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President; in practice the Prime Minister may ask a minister to resign or advise his dismissal.

40.s: With whose consent may a Minister who has resigned explain his resignation in the House through a personal statement?
40.x: A resigned minister may make a personal statement explaining his resignation with the Speaker's consent.

40.x: Ministers hold office at the President's pleasure, but in practice the PM can ask a minister to resign or advise his dismissal.

o: Article 75(2) – Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha

40.s:
With reference to the Union Government, consider the following statements:

40.x: Statement 2 is correct: the Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 on the ARC (1966) recommendation and placed under the PM. 40.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Department of Personnel?

xa: The **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report (1949)** dealt with **reorganising the machinery** of Central Government.
It recommended **grouping ministries** and **cabinet committees**.
**AoB** and **ToB Rules** date from **1961**.

40.s: In which year was the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar report on the reorganisation of the machinery of government submitted?
40.x: The 1949 Ayyangar report dealt with reorganising the machinery of government, including grouping of ministries and Cabinet Committees.
xa: ⚠ It did **not** suggest a minister and secretary solely for administrative reform (UPSC **2021** key).
**ARC (1966)** → **Department of Personnel (1970)**, under the **PM**.

41.s:
Consider the following statements:

o: One sixth of the total members of the House
One tenth of the total members of the House
One fourth of the total members of the House
One third of the total members of the House
41.x: Quorum (Art. 100(3)) is one-tenth of the total members of the House.

xa: Quorum: **one-tenth** (**Art. 100**).
Rules of procedure: **Art. 118**.

41.s: What is the maximum gap allowed between two sessions of Parliament?
41.x: Two sessions cannot be more than six months apart; this keeps legislative business going and the government accountable, though it fixes no minimum sitting days.
xa: This was an **APPSC-GS 2025** question.

**Art. 98**: separate secretariats for each House.

xs: The President summons each House under **Article 85** — option **(2)**.

3. Reassembly in a new session

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: A sitting is a daily meeting of the House during a session.
Prorogation terminates the House itself but not its session.
Dissolution ends the life of the House and applies only to the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment terminates a sitting for a specified period.
41.x: Prorogation ends the session, not the House; only dissolution ends the House, and only the Lok Sabha can be dissolved.
n: A sitting is a daily meeting of a House during a session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Adjournment terminates a daily sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation does not terminate the House itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution ends the life of the House entirely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution applies only to the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The specified period of an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution terminates a House and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: **Adjournment sine die** ends a sitting **without fixing a date** for reassembly.
Adjournment is by the **Presiding Officer**; prorogation by the **President**.
The **Rajya Sabha** is permanent and cannot be dissolved.

41.s: What is the termination of a session of a House, without ending the life of the House, called?
41.x: Prorogation ends the session; adjournment ends a sitting for a set time, adjournment sine die ends it without a date, and dissolution ends the House.
n: Adjournment terminates a daily sitting for a specified time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Adjournment sine die terminates a sitting without assigning a day for reassembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session of the House. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution ends the life of the House entirely. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The specified period of an adjournment may be hours, days, or weeks. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prorogation terminates a session and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Dissolution terminates a House and may be effected by the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: Prorogation usually follows **adjournment sine die**.
**Recess:** period between **prorogation** and a new session.

xs: The quorum is **one-tenth** of the total membership — option **(1)**.

xa: **Art. 98:** separate secretarial staff for each House.
**Art. 118:** rules of procedure; **Art. 120:** language — **Hindi or English**.
Lok Sabha Secretariat is under the **Speaker**; Rajya Sabha Secretariat under the **Chairman**.

41.s: Which House can be dissolved?

41.s: Parliamentary privileges

are available to all persons entitled to speak and take part in the proceedings of a house or any of the committees

41.s: Which Article protects the freedom of speech of members in Parliament?

41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Sita Soren case (2024)?
o: It was decided by a seven-judge Bench.

It held that every speech made by a legislator outside the House is protected by Article 105.

41.x: Sita Soren held no such thing; it held that parliamentary privilege does not protect bribery for voting or speaking.
xa: **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**: Tenth Schedule decisions subject to judicial review.

41.s: What kind of privilege is the right to be informed of a member's arrest, detention or release?

a Fundamental Right of the member under Article 22
a collective privilege of the House
a privilege of the Presiding Officer alone

41.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

n: Fourteen days is the prior-notice period for the impeachment of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 61 governs the prior notice for the President's impeachment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
A President's impeachment notice requires the signatures of at least one-fourth of the members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the period for consideration of a Money Bill by the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 109 governs the Rajya Sabha's consideration of a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
A Money Bill is deemed to have been passed by the Rajya Sabha if the Rajya Sabha does not return it within fourteen days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the period for resolving simultaneous membership of Parliament and a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
The Representation of the People Act, 1951 governs simultaneous membership resignation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Failure to resign a State Legislature seat within fourteen days vacates the person's Parliament seat. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Fourteen days is the notice period for removing the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]
Article 90(c) governs the removal notice for the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 117-120]

xs: The incorrect statement is that the Deputy Chairman's removal notice **requires 30 days** — option **(3)**.
The notice is **fourteen days** — **Article 90(c)**.

xa: **Thirty days:** an Emergency survives **thirty days** from the reconstituted LS's **first sitting** if the **RS approved** it.
**Sixty days:** unauthorised absence under **Article 101(4)**.
The **Speaker's** removal also needs **fourteen days'** notice.

Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority

45.s: What is the quorum for a sitting of a Legislative Assembly of 70 members?

46.s: The Advisory opinion tendered by the Supreme Court of India is

If his party gets largest number of votes in the country
If he secures more votes than any other candidate
If he secures more votes than the sum of votes of all other candidates

65.s: A candidate will lose deposit in an assembly election, if he does not secure
o: More than 1/6th of the valid votes polled
More than 1/5th of the valid votes polled
More than 1/10th of the valid votes polled
More than 1/8th of the valid votes polled

65.s: Which party is called as the Grand Old Party?
65.x:
Most keys: The Republican Party (GOP). Indian media also call the Indian National Congress 'the grand old party'.
'Grand Old Party' (GOP) is the standard nickname of the US Republican Party.

65.s: Vice-President of India is elected by whom?
o: Elected members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Elected members of Parliament and State Assemblies
All members (elected and nominated) of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
65.src: APPSC Junior Steno's in AP Vaidhya Vidhana Parishad 2012
65.x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (All members (elected and nominated) of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha); it is added as option 5.
The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college of all members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated (Art. 66). 'Elected members' only is wrong, and State Assemblies have no role (they vote only for the President).

65.s: The Constitutional Amendment Act which lowered down the voting age from 21 years to 18 years is
65.x: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18.

65.s: Right to vote is:
65.x: The right to vote is a political right (participation in government). In India it is a statutory right (Sec. 62, RP Act 1951), not a Fundamental Right.

65.s: Which of the following Constitution Amendment Acts reduced the minimum age for voting from 21 to 18 years?
65.x: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18; the 73rd is Panchayati Raj.

65.s:
Which of the election system have been adopted for different elections in India?
(1) Direct Election System on the basis of Adult Suffrage.
(2) System of Proportional representation by a Single Transferable Vote.
(3) List System of Proportional Representation.
(4) The cumulative Voting system of Indirect Election.
Choose the correct answer from the given code-
65.x: Direct election on adult suffrage and PR by single transferable vote are used in India; the list system and cumulative voting are not.

65.s: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides right to vote i.e. adult suffrage for electing representatives of Lok Saba and Vidhan Sabha?
65.x: Art. 326 provides adult suffrage for the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections.

65.s: The uniform adult FRANCHISE system has been adopted
o: To provide a right to vote to all the citizens of India. Subject to limitations conferred by statute
To cater to the needs of senior citizens of India
To guarantee employment for at least one person in a family
To provide uniform health care system in India
65.x: Universal adult franchise gives every citizen aged 18+ the vote, subject to disqualifications by law (non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, corrupt practice; Art. 326).

65.s: Under first-past-the-post in Lok Sabha elections, how does a candidate win?
o: At least two-thirds of the valid votes
More than half of the valid votes
At least one-third of the valid votes
65.x: FPTP needs only a plurality in a single-member constituency, not a majority.
xa: FPTP (territorial, single-member) is used for the **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies**.
PR was rejected for Lok Sabha as hard for voters and prone to **fragmentation and unstable** governments.
**Security deposit** is forfeited below **one-sixth** of valid votes.

65.s: The State Legislative Assembly is elected from which type of constituencies?
65.x: Assembly members are directly elected from single-member territorial constituencies, by first-past-the-post.
n: The Legislative Assembly is elected from single-member territorial constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The Legislative Assembly is directly elected by the people. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xs: The Assembly is elected from **single-member territorial constituencies** — option **(4)**.
It is **directly elected** by citizens using **First-Past-the-Post**.
xa: It rests on **universal adult suffrage** — **Article 326**.
Conducted by the **Election Commission of India** (**Article 324**).
Assembly is under **Article 170**.

65.s: Which of the following was cited as a reason for rejecting proportional representation for Lok Sabha elections?
o: It guarantees direct election in every single-member constituency
It may lead to unstable governments
It reduces the cost of elections
65.x: Unstable governments, fragmentation, expense, difficulty for voters and a weaker voter–MP link were cited against PR; guaranteeing direct election in single-member seats is not such a reason.

65.s: Which of the following statements about NOTA in Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections is incorrect?
o: NOTA continues to be applicable in these elections because they are indirect elections.
NOTA is not applicable in Rajya Sabha elections.
NOTA is not applicable in Legislative Council elections.
The Supreme Court struck down NOTA in these elections in 2018.
65.x: Option A is incorrect: the Supreme Court struck down NOTA for Rajya Sabha and Council elections in 2018. NOTA applies only to direct Lok Sabha and Assembly elections.
65.tq: Recall the 2018 ruling on indirect elections.
n: NOTA is not applicable in Rajya Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is not applicable in Legislative Council elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
The Supreme Court struck down NOTA for Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections in 2018. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is limited to direct Lok Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is limited to direct Assembly elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **NOTA continues to apply** in Rajya Sabha and Council elections — option **(1)**.
The **Supreme Court struck down** NOTA for **Rajya Sabha** and **Legislative Council** elections in **2018**.
NOTA is limited to **direct Lok Sabha** and **Assembly** elections.
xa: Rajya Sabha and Councils use **PR-STV** (indirect).
NOTA symbol: ballot with a black cross by **NID, Ahmedabad**.
NOTA first used in the Lok Sabha in **2014**.

65.s: Who elects the Vice-President of India?
65.x: The Vice-President is elected by all MPs, elected and nominated, by single transferable vote; the President by elected MPs and MLAs.
n: The President is elected through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Vice-President is elected through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Citizens directly elect Lok Sabha members from territorial electoral rolls. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Lok Sabha uses the first-past-the-post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of the Legislative Assemblies of the respective States elect Rajya Sabha members. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Rajya Sabha is elected indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Rajya Sabha uses proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The President is elected by elected Members of Parliament and elected Members of Legislative Assemblies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Vice-President is elected by all Members of Parliament, both elected and nominated. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of Parliament form part of the Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
All Members of Parliament form the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of Parliament form part of the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Nominated Members of Parliament form part of the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xa: Articles: President **54**; Vice-President **66**; Lok Sabha **81**; Rajya Sabha **80**.
Delhi and Puducherry MLAs join the presidential electoral college (**70th Constitutional Amendment Act**).
**Legislative Councils** also use PR-STV.

65.s: Under which Article is the Vice-President elected?
65.x: The Vice-President is elected under Article 66; the President under Article 54.
n: The President is elected under Article 54. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Vice-President is elected under Article 66. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Lok Sabha is constituted under Article 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Legislative Assembly is provided for under Article 170. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Legislative Council is provided for under Article 171. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xa: **Rajya Sabha** = **Article 80**.
**Lok Sabha** and **Assembly** use **FPTP**; the rest use **PR-STV**.
Panchayat/municipal members: minimum age **21**.

65.s: Which of the following has no role in the election of the Vice-President of India?
65.x: The Vice-President is elected only by MPs of both Houses, elected and nominated; State Legislatures have no role.
n: State Legislative Assembly members have no role in electing the Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
State Legislative Council members have no role in electing the Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The Vice-President is elected by all Members of Parliament, both elected and nominated. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
All Members of Parliament form the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of Parliament form part of the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Nominated Members of Parliament form part of the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
State Legislatures are completely excluded from the Vice-Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]

65.s: Under Article 326, on which grounds may a citizen aged 18 or above be disqualified from voting?
o: Non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime or corrupt practice
65.x: Article 326 grants adult suffrage subject to disqualifications such as non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime and corrupt or illegal practice.
xa: Voting age was cut from **21 to 18** by the **61st Amendment Act, 1988**.
Right to vote is a **statutory right**, not a Fundamental Right.

65.s: Which is the constitutional authority for conducting State Legislative Assembly elections?
65.x: Assembly elections are direct, use first-past-the-post and are run by the Election Commission of India.
n: Citizens directly elect the State Legislative Assembly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
State Legislative Assembly elections are conducted on the basis of universal adult suffrage under Article 326. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
State Legislative Assembly elections use the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
The Election Commission of India conducts elections to the State Legislative Assembly under Article 324. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 104-108]
xa: ⚠ Assembly polls are run by the ECI, **not** the State Election Commission.
Members come from **single-member territorial constituencies**.
FPTP needs no absolute majority over **50 percent**.

65.s: Which Amendment Act lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 years?
65.x: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 lowered the voting age to 18.
n: The voting age was lowered from 21 years to 18 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988, lowered the voting age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The minimum age for membership of a Legislative Council is 30 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
The minimum age for Panchayat and Municipality elections is 21 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xa: The change became effective in **1989** (some notes say 1987).
Right to vote is a **statutory right** (**Kuldip Nayar, 2006**).
**Article 326** = universal adult suffrage.

65.s: A candidate forfeits the security deposit on securing not more than what share of the valid votes?
65.x: A candidate with one-sixth or less of the valid votes forfeits the deposit.
n: NOTA does not determine the election outcome by itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Under NOTA, the candidate with the highest valid votes among the contestants is declared elected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Abstention under old Rule 49-O did not affect the winning tally. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
Under the international right to reject, re-election is mandated if rejection crosses a threshold of more than 50%. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xa: ⚠ Trap: "election cancelled if NOTA gets the highest votes" is **false**.
NOTA applies only to **direct Lok Sabha** and **Assembly** elections.
**PUCL** judgment: **27 September 2013**.

65.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The right to vote is a Fundamental Right.
2. The right to contest an election is a statutory right.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
65.x: The right to vote is statutory, not fundamental; the right to contest is also statutory (Kuldip Nayar, 2006).
n: The right to contest elections is a legal or statutory right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to vote is not a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to vote is a legal or statutory right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The Supreme Court established the statutory nature of the right to vote and the right to contest in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India in 2006. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
The right to contest elections is not a Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 141-144]
xa: Basis: **RPA 1950 Section 19** and **RPA 1951**.
**Article 326** gives the vote to every citizen aged **18+** unless disqualified.

65.s: Which additional areas are included in the Presidential electoral college through the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act?
o: Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
65.x: The 70th Amendment (1992) added the elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry to the electoral college for the President.
n: Elected Members of the Delhi Legislative Assembly form part of the Presidential electoral college through the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of the Puducherry Legislative Assembly form part of the Presidential electoral college through the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
Elected Members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 91-94]
xs: The **70th Constitutional Amendment Act** added **Delhi and Puducherry** to the President's electoral college — option **(1)**.
Their **elected** MLAs vote with **elected** MPs and **elected** members of State Assemblies.
xa: President is elected under **Article 54** by **PR-STV**, **secret ballot**.
**Nominated** members do not vote for the President but do vote for the **Vice-President**.
Vice-President: **Article 66**.

65.s: Which of the following describes an Electronic Voting Machine?
o: A judicial mechanism for resolving election disputes
An electoral system based on proportional representation
An electronic vote recording and counting apparatus
65.x: An EVM is a machine that records and counts votes. It is not an electoral system; first-past-the-post is the system.
65.tq: Discriminate a voting machine from an electoral system.
n: An EVM is an electronic vote-recording apparatus. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
An EVM is an electronic vote-counting apparatus. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
An EVM is not an electoral system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
xs: An **EVM** is an **electronic vote-recording and vote-counting apparatus** — option **(4)**.
⚠ It is **not** an **electoral system**; India's system for direct elections is **First-Past-the-Post**.
xa: EVMs are used for **Lok Sabha** and **State Assembly** elections.
Deployed under the **superintendence, direction and control** of the **ECI**.
First EVM: **Parur 1982**; VVPAT: **Noksen 2013**.

65.s: NOTA is NOT applicable in which of the following elections?
65.x: NOTA does not apply to Rajya Sabha or Legislative Council elections.
n: NOTA is an electoral option provided on ballot papers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is an electoral option provided on Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA enables voters to formally reject all contesting candidates in secret. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is a symbolic expression only. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA does not determine the election outcome by itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is not applicable in Rajya Sabha elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
NOTA is not applicable in Legislative Council elections. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 176-178]
xa: NOTA came from **PUCL v. Union of India** (**2013**).
NOTA first Lok Sabha use: **2014** — **1.1%** of votes.
⚠ NOTA is not **abstention**.

65.s: A candidate can win a State Assembly election without getting more than 50 per cent of the votes. Which system makes this possible?
o: Proportional representation by single transferable vote
65.x: Under first-past-the-post, the candidate with the most valid votes wins even without 50 per cent.
n: The Legislative Assembly election uses the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
A candidate does not need an absolute majority of more than 50 percent to win under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
The candidate securing the highest number of valid votes wins under the First-Past-the-Post system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #60 · pp 158-161]
xa: FPTP is used for the **Lok Sabha** and **Assemblies**.
**PR-STV** is used for **Rajya Sabha**, **Legislative Councils**, **President** and **Vice-President**.
PR was rejected for the Lok Sabha due to **fragmentation and unstable** governments.

65.s: What is the minimum age for a citizen to contest a Lok Sabha election?
65.x: A Lok Sabha candidate must be a citizen on the electoral roll of a constituency and at least 25 years old.

65.s: By whom are the members of the Rajya Sabha from the States elected?
o: Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
Members of the State Legislative Councils
All members of the Lok Sabha

65.s: What is the minimum age to contest elections to Panchayats and Municipalities?
65.x: The minimum age to be a member of a Panchayat or Municipality is 21 years.

65.s: Which of the following statements is/are correct? i. Floating Constituencies are the constituencies without fixed geographical borders. ii. In the constituency of Sangha in Sikkim, only Buddhist monks can contest and vote. the B.' dir C. Rig
65.x: A floating constituency has no fixed geographical boundary; Sangha (Sikkim) is the example where only registered Buddhist monks vote and contest. Both are correct.

65.s: What is an election held after a legislature is dissolved before the end of its normal term called?
65.x: A mid-term election follows premature dissolution; a by-election fills a single vacancy, ordinarily within six months.
xa: Bypoll exceptions: remaining term **under one year**, or ECI (consulting the Centre) certifies difficulty.
The first four general elections (**1951-52, 1957, 1962, 1967**) were **simultaneous** with Assembly polls.

65.s: In which of the following cases does the six-month rule for holding a by-election NOT apply?
o: The vacancy arises in a reserved constituency
The vacancy arises from the resignation of the member
The vacancy arises during a session of the House
The remaining term is less than one year
65.x: The exceptions are a remaining term of less than one year, or the Election Commission certifying difficulty after consulting the Central Government.
xa: By-election = **single vacancy**, within **6 months** (**Sec. 151A RPA**).
A polling station may have at most **1,200 electors**.

65.s: What is a constituency with no fixed geographical boundary, such as the Sangha seat in Sikkim, called?
65.x: A floating constituency has no fixed geographical boundary. The Sangha constituency in Sikkim is an example in which only registered Buddhist monks vote and contest.
65.tq: Identify the exact electoral term from its defining geographical feature.
xs: A seat with no fixed geographical boundary is a **floating constituency** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Sangha (Sikkim)** — only **registered Buddhist monks** vote and contest.
xa: PYQ: APPSC-G2 **2023, 2025** — both statements on floating constituency were correct.
**Delimitation** fixes the **number of seats and boundaries** of territorial constituencies.

65.s: In which of the Lok Sabha elections held in the years given below highest voter turnout was recorded?

2014 was the record then — now 2019 holds the highest Lok Sabha turnout, 67.4% (ECI).

65.s: The single party type of government in India ended after the Lok Sabha Elections held in
65.x:
single-party majorities returned in 2014 (BJP 282) and 2019 (303) — now (2024) again no single-party majority (BJP 240, NDA government) (Laxmikanth Table 81.1; ECI 2024)
After the 1989 election no party won a Lok Sabha majority until 2014; minority and coalition governments began (National Front). The 1977 Janata Party was itself a single party with a majority.

65.s: So far, the highest percentage of votes polled was in the Lok Sabha Elections held in
65.x:
