66.x: Assembly candidates in larger States may spend ₹40 lakh (earlier ₹28 lakh); ₹95 lakh is the Lok Sabha limit.

66.s: What is the expenditure limit for a Lok Sabha candidate in a smaller State or UT?
66.x: Smaller States/UTs have a Lok Sabha limit of ₹75 lakh (earlier ₹54 lakh).

66.s: Candidate expenditure limits are prescribed under Rule 90 of which of the following?
66.x: Limits are fixed under Rule 90, Conduct of Election Rules 1961, raised by the 2022 Amendment Rules.

66.s: By which of the following were candidate expenditure limits raised to ₹95 lakh (Lok Sabha) and ₹40 lakh (Assembly) in larger States?
66.x: Limits under Rule 90 of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961 were raised by the Conduct of Elections (Amendment) Rules, 2022.

66.s: According to ADR, about what share of political parties' funds in 2004-23 came from undisclosed sources?
66.x: ADR found that 60% (₹19,083 crore) of party funds in 2004-23 came from undisclosed sources.

66.s: Under which Section of the Income-tax Act, 2025 do political parties get tax exemption?
66.x: Party tax exemption is now in Section 12 of the Income-tax Act, 2025; earlier it was Section 13A of the 1961 Act.

66.s: What was the Supreme Court of India ruling on the Electoral Bond Scheme?
o: The scheme was uphold as constitutional
The scheme was struck down as unconstitutional
The scheme was modified to include more transparency measures
The scheme was deferred for further reviews
66.src: APPSC General Studies & Mental Ability (Common Paper for Var
66.x: In ADR v Union of India (15 Feb 2024) a five-judge bench unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional, as it violated voters' right to information under Art. 19(1)(a).

66.s:
Consider the following Statements about 'Electoral Bonds'

A. A citizen of India or a body incorporated in India will be eligible to purchase the Electoral Bonds

B. Electoral Bonds would be purchased for any value of Rs 1000 maximum up to 1 crore from specified branches of State Bank of India.

C. Electoral Bonds would have a life of only 15 days during which it can be used for making donations only to political parties registered under section 29A of Representation of People Act 1951.

D. Electoral bonds are donated to a political party which secured not less than 1% of votes polled in the last general assembly elections.
Which of the above statement is/are correct?
66.x: All four are correct: bonds could be bought by a citizen or a body incorporated in India, in values from Rs 1,000 to Rs 1 crore at SBI, were valid for 15 days, and could go only to a 29A-registered party with at least 1% of the votes in the last election.

66.s:
Consider following statements about Electoral Bond Scheme 2018:
(A) The aim of this scheme is to bring about transparency in the funding process of political parties.
(B) Only the political parties recognized by the Election Commission which secured not less than two percent of the votes polled in the last general election to the House of People or the Legislative Assembly of the State shall be eligible to receive the Electoral Bonds.
(C) Electoral Bonds shall be valid for fifteen calendar days from the date of issue.
(D) The Electoral Bond deposited by an eligible political party in its account shall be credited on the same day.
Which of the above statements are correct?
66.x: Aim (transparency), the 15-day validity and same-day credit are correct. The eligibility threshold was not less than 1% of the votes in the last Lok Sabha or Assembly election, not 2%.

66.s: In ADR v Union of India (2024), on what main ground did the Supreme Court strike down the Electoral Bond Scheme?
o: The right to equality under Article 14
The voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a)
The right to life under Article 21
The freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c)
66.x: The five-judge bench unanimously held that donor anonymity violated voters' right to information, part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Articles 14, 21 and 19(1)(c) were not the ground stated for striking the scheme down.
66.tq: Bonds struck down = Art 19(1)(a) right to information (15 Feb 2024).
xs: The scheme violated voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(2)**.
Articles **14**, **21** and **19(1)(c)** were not the stated ground.
xa: **PUCL (2003)**: voter's **right to know** is part of Art. 19(1)(a).
**PUCL (2013)**: right to reject (NOTA) also flows from Art. 19(1)(a).

66.s: The Supreme Court's decision in Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India also invalidated which change associated with electoral political funding?
o: Abolition of political party registration under the RPA
Removal of the corporate donation cap under the Companies Act
Compulsory disclosure of all cash donations by parties
Restriction on donations by individual citizens
66.x: The Court struck down the removal of the corporate donation cap from the Companies Act.
66.tq: Identify the allied legal provision affected by the judgment, not merely the main scheme.
xs: It also struck down the **removal of the corporate donation cap** from the **Companies Act** — option **(2)**.
The notes record no ruling on party registration, cash disclosure or individual donations.
xa: Ground: violation of voters' **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
ADR: **60% (₹19,083 cr)** of party funds in **2004-23** came from undisclosed sources.

66.s: A political party could encash electoral bonds only if it had secured at least what percentage of votes in the last election?
66.x: Only a registered political party that had secured at least 1% of the votes in the last election could encash electoral bonds.
66.tq: Recall the statutory eligibility threshold rather than the general registration requirement.
xs: A party could encash electoral bonds only with at least **1 per cent** (**1% of the vote**) in the last election — so option **(2)** is correct.
Only **registered parties** meeting this **1%** threshold could encash; the bonds were sold only by **SBI** as **bearer bonds**.
xa: Denominations: **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore**; each bond was valid for **15 days**.
The scheme was notified in **2018** via **Finance Act 2017** amendments.
Struck down as **unconstitutional** by a unanimous **five-judge Constitution Bench** in **ADR v UoI** (**15 Feb 2024**) — it violated the **right to information under Art. 19(1)(a)**.
⚠ Donor anonymity was hailed in older notes as a "**transparency**" gain.

66.s: In the 2024 electoral bond judgment, whom did the Supreme Court direct to give donor data to the Election Commission?
66.x: A five-judge Constitution Bench unanimously struck down the scheme and directed SBI to provide donor data to the ECI.
xa: Case: **ADR v Union of India, 15 Feb 2024**.
⚠ **ADR v UoI** 2002 = disclosure; **ADR v ECI** 2024 = EVM/VVPAT.

66.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about electoral bonds?
o: They were sold only by the State Bank of India
They were issued in denominations from ₹1,000 to ₹10 crore
66.x: The denominations ran from ₹1,000 to ₹1 crore, not ₹10 crore; SBI was the only seller and the bearer bonds were valid for 15 days.

66.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 2013 — Lily Thomas judgment striking down Section 8(4) of the RPA
2002 — Disclosure of criminal record, assets and education
66.x: Electoral bonds were struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024; they were not introduced in that year. The other pairs are correctly matched.
66.tq: Find the reversed action-year pair, particularly where a later year records invalidation rather than introduction.
xs: **2024 — Introduction of electoral bonds** is wrongly matched — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Electoral bonds were notified in **2018** and **struck down** in **2024** (**ADR v UoI**, **15 Feb 2024**).
The rest are correct: **Lily Thomas** struck down **Sec. 8(4)** in **2013**; **ADR v UoI** (**2002**) mandated disclosure; **EVMs** in all constituencies in **2004**.
xa: ⚠ **ADR v UoI** **2002** = disclosure; **2024** = electoral bonds; **ADR v ECI** **2024** = EVM/VVPAT.
Bonds were sold only by **SBI**, in **₹1,000 to ₹1 crore** denominations, valid **15 days**.
The verdict was by a unanimous **five-judge Constitution Bench**, under the **right to information** (**Art. 19(1)(a)**).

66.s: Who could buy electoral bonds?
o: Only companies listed on a stock exchange
A citizen of India or a body incorporated in India
66.x: Bonds could be bought by a citizen of India or a body incorporated in India, alone or jointly.

66.s: On which date was the Electoral Bond Scheme notified?
66.x: The scheme was notified on 2 January 2018 and struck down on 15 February 2024.

66.s: By which bench was the 2024 electoral bonds verdict in ADR v Union of India delivered?
66.x: A five-judge bench unanimously held the scheme unconstitutional.

66.s: Through which law was the Electoral Bond Scheme brought in?
66.x: The Electoral Bond Scheme was notified on 2 January 2018 on the basis of the Finance Act, 2017.

66.s: 'Government funding of Parliamentary Elections' was recommended by
66.x: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) recommended (partial, in kind) government funding of Parliamentary elections; the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) later examined State funding in detail. Venkatachaliah headed the NCRWC, not an election-funding body.

66.s: The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended:
o: The constitution of state-level election commission
List system of election to the Lok Sabha
A ban on the candidature of independent candidates
66.x: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) recommended government funding of Parliamentary elections (in kind); its other proposals led to the RP (Amendment) Act, 1996. It did not propose a list system or a ban on independents.

66.s: In what form did the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) recommend State funding of elections?
o: Partial funding in kind to recognised parties and candidates
Full funding in cash to every candidate
Full funding in kind to every candidate
Partial cash funding to independents only
66.x: It suggested partial funding in kind to recognised parties and candidates; the recommendation is still not adopted.
xa: ⚠ "Which is NOT on Centre-State relations?" → **Indrajit Gupta**.
APPSC **2025**: Indrajit Gupta = electoral reforms.

66.s: On which condition did the Law Commission's 170th Report find full State funding of elections desirable?
o: Only recognised parties were allowed to contest
Parties were barred from taking funds from other sources
Independent candidates were excluded from funding
66.x: The Law Commission considered full state funding desirable only if parties were barred from receiving funds from other sources.
xa: The **170th Report** also backed **simultaneous elections**, **internal party democracy** and partial **list (PR) seats**.
**Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998)**: partial funding **in kind** to recognised parties/candidates; still **not adopted**.
**Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** and the **2nd ARC** also recommended public funding.
Countries with public funding: **Germany, Sweden, Japan** (and **Canada** in another list).

66.s: The 'level field for resource-poor candidates' argument for State funding of elections rests on equality under which Article?
66.x: The level-field argument rests on equality under Article 14; curbing black money is another argument in favour, while the fiscal burden is an argument against.
xa: Another objection: it does **not stop off-book cash** spending.
SC (**2026**): eliminating black money is a **core ECI responsibility**.

66.s: According to the Supreme Court decision in State of Karnataka v. Prathik Parasrampuria (2026), eliminating black money from elections is primarily whose core responsibility?
66.x: The Supreme Court described elimination of black money from elections as a core responsibility of the Election Commission of India.
66.tq: Ask which constitutional institution has the responsibility, avoiding a swap with an auditing or fiscal body.
xs: In **State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria (2026)**, the SC called eliminating black money from elections a **core responsibility** of the **Election Commission of India** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The case is on the **state funding** page; the CAG, Parliament Secretariat and Finance Commission are not named for this role.
xa: Yet the ECI still **lacks power to deregister** parties for **financial non-compliance**.
The **Law Commission 255th Report (2015)** sought **limited power to deregister** non-compliant parties.
Arguments for state funding: curbs **black money** and quid-pro-quo funding; levels the field (**Art. 14**).
Against: **heavy fiscal burden**; does not stop **off-book cash** spending.

66.s: What is the State funding model called in which the State bears all legitimate costs and private donations are banned?
66.x: Bearing all legitimate costs while banning private donations describes full funding; funding may be full or partial, in cash or in kind.
xa: Countries with public funding: **Germany, Sweden, Japan** (+ **Canada**).
Against: **heavy fiscal burden**; does not stop **off-book cash**.

66.s:
Consider the following statements about State funding of elections:
1. Germany, Sweden, Japan and Canada practise it.
2. Under full State funding, private donations are banned.
3. The Indrajit Gupta Committee's recommendation was adopted.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
66.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; the Indrajit Gupta Committee's recommendation of partial funding was not adopted.

66.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the VVPAT (Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trial) machines used by Election Commission of India?

a. VVPAT system gives instant feedback to the voter showing that the vote polled has in fact been allotted against the candidate chosen.

b. A voter-verified paper audit trial was first used in an election in India in 2013 in Nagaland.

66.s: Which provision of law enables the Election Commission of India to use Electronic Voting Machines in Polls?
o: Article 328 of the Constitution of India
Article 329 of the Constitution of India
Section 61A of the Representation of Peoples' Act
Section 61(a) of the Representation of Peoples' Act

66.x: Section 61A of the RPA, 1951 (inserted in 1989) enables the ECI to use EVMs. Arts. 328/329 deal with State election laws and the bar on courts.

o: Subramanian Swamy Vs Union of India
Arun Jaitley Vs Union of India

66.s:
Which of the following statements is / are not true regarding Electronic Voting Machines (EVM)?
A. EVMS were used for the first time in the entire State of Goa in the general elections to the Assembly in 1999.
B. EVMs were used for the first time on experimental basis in the selected constituencies in the Assembly elections to the States of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat in 1998.
o: Both A and B are true
66.x: A is true: Goa (1999) was the first State to hold its entire Assembly election on EVMs. B is false: the 1998 trial was in Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Delhi, not Gujarat. So only B is not true.

66.s:
Consider the following Election Reforms in India and arrange them in correct chronological order starting from earliest to the last.
1. Voters photo identity card
2. Electronic voting machine
3. Voter verifiable paper audit trail
4. NOTA
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
66.x: EVM (Parur, 1982) → EPIC (1993) → VVPAT (Noksen, 4 Sep 2013) → NOTA (PUCL judgment 27 Sep 2013, used from Nov 2013).

66.s: What is the version of the machine VVPAT used for voting in India?
66.x: The M3 (third-generation) EVMs and VVPATs are used in India; they have tamper detection and self-diagnostics.

66.s: What is a totaliser, which combines the counting of several EVMs, meant to do?
66.x: A totaliser combines several EVM counts to hide booth-wise trends; the ECI stated no legal framework for it exists.
xa: Recommended by the **Law Commission 255th Report (2015)**.
SC **sought the Centre's response** on totalisers as a "fall-back option" (**Sep 2026**).

66.s: Where is ECIL, one of the two public sector undertakings that make EVMs, headquartered?
66.x: BEL is based in Bengaluru and ECIL in Hyderabad.
xa: BEL and ECIL also make **VVPATs**.
AP angle: **ECIL** is the EVM maker based in **Hyderabad**.

66.s: Under ADR v. ECI (2024), for how long are symbol-loading units to be sealed and kept?
66.x: The Court rejected ballot papers and 100% VVPAT counting, but ordered SLUs preserved for 45 days and allowed runners-up to seek checking of 5% of EVMs.
xa: The check is of the EVMs' **burnt memory**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)** raised the VVPAT tally to **5** polling stations per segment.

66.s: Which case held that VVPAT is necessary for free and fair elections and directed its introduction in phases?
o: State of Karnataka v Prathik Parasrampuria
66.x: In Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013), the Supreme Court held that VVPAT was needed for free and fair polls and required phased introduction.
66.tq: Match the judicial case with its distinctive electoral reform.
xs: **Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)** held VVPAT needed for free and fair polls, to be brought **in phases** — option **(1)**.
**ADR v ECI** = 2024 EVM/VVPAT safeguards; **PUCL** = NOTA; **Prathik Parasrampuria** = black money.
xa: VVPAT debuted at **Noksen**, **2013**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2019)**: tally from **1 to 5** polling stations per segment.

66.s: In ADR v ECI (2024), how did the Supreme Court respond to the demand to return to paper ballots?
o: Ordered a return to paper ballots
Refused to order a return to paper ballots
66.x: The Supreme Court refused to order a return to paper ballots and has repeatedly upheld the use of EVMs.

66.s: How did N. Chandrababu Naidu v Union of India (2019) change the random VVPAT-EVM tally?
o: Two to five polling stations per district
One to five polling stations per Assembly segment
One to ten polling stations per parliamentary constituency
Five to ten polling stations per Assembly segment
66.x: The 2019 decision raised the random VVPAT-EVM tally from one to five polling stations per Assembly segment.
66.tq: Remember both sides of the judicially ordered numerical increase.
xs: **N. Chandrababu Naidu v UoI (2019)** raised the random VVPAT–EVM tally from **one to five polling stations** per **Assembly segment** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The tally unit is the **Assembly segment**, not a district or parliamentary constituency.
xa: **ADR v ECI (Apr 2024)** rejected **100% slip counting** and a **return to paper ballots**.
In that case, symbol-loading units are sealed for **45 days**; runners-up can seek a check of **5% of EVMs**.
**Subramanian Swamy v ECI (2013)**: VVPAT is needed for free and fair polls; introduce it **in phases**.

66.s: VVPAT slips must be counted in which of the following circumstances?
o: Whenever EVM data and Form 17C do not match
Whenever postal ballots exceed the number of EVM votes
Only in constituencies using postal ballots
Only when the winning candidate requests it after the declaration of results
66.x: VVPAT slips are required to be counted wherever the EVM data and Form 17C do not match.
66.tq: Apply the verification rule to a specific discrepancy rather than to a general recount demand.
xs: **VVPAT slips must be counted wherever EVM data do not match Form 17C** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is one of the **new ECI rules** on counting; postal ballots relate to a different rule (below).
xa: The **penultimate EVM/VVPAT round** is counted only after **postal ballots** are finished.
**ADR v ECI (April 2024)**: candidates placed **2nd and 3rd** can seek a check of **5% of EVMs' burnt memory** within **7 days**.
ECI objects that **totalisers** would make **EVM, VVPAT and Form 17C** checks harder.

66.s: Which State was the first to conduct its entire Assembly election using EVMs?
66.x: Goa conducted the first whole-State Assembly election using EVMs in 1999. Gujarat was not the first State to do so.
66.tq: Separate pilot use from the first whole-State use.
xs: **Goa, 1999** was the first whole-State Assembly election on EVMs — option **(2)**.
⚠ **Gujarat** was **not** the first; **Kerala** (**Parur 1982**) was the first pilot; **Nagaland** (Noksen) = first **VVPAT**.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2025** key: the Goa 1999 statement is true.
**2004** = first nationwide (all-India) EVM use.

66.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
66.x: VVPAT was introduced on 4 September 2013; EVMs were first used on 19 May 1982, EPIC rolled out in 1993 and NOTA on 27 September 2013.
n: Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) were first used experimentally on 19 May 1982. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
Electors Photo Identity Cards (EPICs) had their nationwide rollout initiated in 1993. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
The Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) was first used on 4 September 2013. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
None of the Above (NOTA) was implemented on 27 September 2013. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
VVPAT was introduced before NOTA in 2013. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
NOTA was mandated later in September 2013 than VVPAT was introduced. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
xa: ⚠ **VVPAT** came **before NOTA** in **2013**.
**Section 61A** (RPA 1951) gave EVMs statutory backing in **1989**.
**2004** = first all-EVM Lok Sabha election.

66.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Goa (1999) – First State-wide Assembly election using EVMs
Parur Assembly Constituency – First experimental use of EVM
14th Lok Sabha election (2004) – First nationwide general election entirely using EVMs
66.x: VVPAT was first introduced in Noksen Assembly Constituency; Goa saw the first all-EVM State poll.
n: The first experimental use of EVMs occurred in the Parur Assembly Constituency in Kerala. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
The first VVPAT use occurred in the Noksen Assembly Constituency in Nagaland. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
Goa was the first State to conduct an entire General Assembly election using EVMs across all constituencies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
The 14th Lok Sabha General Election in 2004 was the first nationwide general election conducted entirely using EVMs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 199-201]
xa: ⚠ **Gujarat** was **not** the first State to use EVMs in an Assembly election.
Noksen VVPAT use was a **by-election** on **4 September 2013**.
EVM makers: **BEL** (Bengaluru) and **ECIL** (Hyderabad).

66.s: At how many electors per polling station did the Election Commission fix the cap?
66.x: The ECI capped the number of electors per polling station at 1,200, down from the earlier 1,500.

55.s: Who appoints the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
55.x: The President appoints the CAG (Art. 148(1)).

55.s: Comptroller and Auditor General of India is
55.x:
Vinod Rai's term ended in 2013 — now K. Sanjay Murthy is CAG (since 21 November 2024) (Praveen CA360 Jun 2026)
Vinod Rai was CAG from January 2008 to May 2013. (now K. Sanjay Murthy, since 21 Nov 2024)

55.s: The State Finance Commission is appointed by
55.x: The State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor (i.e. the State Government) every five years under Art. 243I.

55.s: Among the following whose term of office is the longest?
55.x: The CAG serves 6 years or till 65; the President, Vice-President and a Lok Sabha member have 5-year terms.

55.s: In the Indian Order of Precedence, who amongst the following comes first?
o: The Chief Justice of High Court
55.x:
Most keys: CAG. Strictly, the CAG, the Chief Election Commissioner and the UPSC Chairperson share entry 9A of the Table of Precedence; only the High Court Chief Justice (14) ranks lower.
The CAG is at 9A of the Table of Precedence, above Chief Justices of High Courts (14); the MPPSC key took the CAG as first, but he shares 9A with the UPSC Chairperson and the CEC.

55.s: The office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India was created –
o: Through an Act of the Parliament
55.x: The CAG is an independent constitutional authority created by Article 148, not by an Act or a Cabinet resolution.

55.s: The power to grant or refuse leave to the Comptroller and Auditor General shall vest in the
55.x: Leave of the CAG is granted or refused by the President.

55.s: Who is called the Guardian of Public Purse?
55.x: The CAG is called the guardian of the public purse (Art. 148).

55.s: C.A.G. (Comptroller and Auditor General) of India acts as
o: The Chief Legal Advisor of the Government
55.x: The CAG acts as the guardian of public finance (public purse); the Attorney General is the chief legal adviser.

55.s: The salary of the CAG of India, charged on the Consolidated Fund, is equal to that of whom?
55.x: The CAG gets a salary equal to a Supreme Court judge's, charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and not subject to vote.
xa: Salary, **leave**, pension and retirement age cannot be varied to his disadvantage.
Office expenses, allowances and pensions are also **charged** on the CFI.
**Leave** is granted by the **President**.

55.s: Where in the Constitution are the provisions on the Comptroller and Auditor General of India contained?
55.x: The CAG is in Part V, Chapter V, Articles 148–151. Part XII is finance, and Chapter VI is not the CAG chapter.
55.tq: Recall Part V Chapter V for the CAG.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is governed under Part V, Chapter V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Articles 148 to 151 deal with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The CAG is in **Part V, Chapter V, Articles 148–151** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is an **independent constitutional authority**; Part XII and Chapter VI are wrong.
xa: **148** = appointment; **149** = duties and powers; **150** = form of accounts; **151** = audit reports.
Full name: **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India** (not "Controller").
Governing Act: **CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971**.

55.s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the audit reports of the Union and the States?
55.x: Article 151 deals with audit reports; 148 provides for the CAG, 149 his duties and powers, and 150 the form of accounts.
n: Article 148 deals with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 149 deals with the duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 150 deals with the form of accounts of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 151(1) deals with the audit reports of the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Article 151(2) deals with the audit reports of the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: **Article 150:** form prescribed by the **President** on the CAG's **advice**.
Ultimate action rests with **Parliament** / **State Legislature**.

55.s: On whose advice does the President prescribe the form of accounts of the Union and the States?
55.x: Under Article 150, the President prescribes the form of accounts on the CAG's advice.
n: The President prescribes the form of Union and State accounts on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General advises on the form of accounts but does not prescribe it unilaterally. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Union and State accounts are kept in the form prescribed by the President upon the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: The CAG does **not** prescribe it unilaterally.
**Article 149** = duties and powers; **Article 151** = audit reports.
The **1976** reform separated accounting from auditing.

55.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The CAG is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department.
The CAG is a statutory authority functioning under the Ministry of Finance.
The CAG is an independent constitutional authority.
The CAG is designated as the Guardian of the Public Purse.
55.x: B is incorrect: the CAG is an independent constitutional authority (Article 148), not a statutory body under the Finance Ministry. He heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and is the 'guardian of the public purse'.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is an independent constitutional authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is designated as the Guardian of the Public Purse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is the head of the Indian Audit and Accounts Department. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xs: The incorrect statement is that the CAG is a **statutory authority under the Ministry of Finance** — option **(2)**.
The CAG is an **independent constitutional authority** (**Articles 148 to 151**).
It heads the **Indian Audit and Accounts Department** and is the **Guardian of the Public Purse**.
xa: **No minister** represents the CAG in Parliament.
**Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called the CAG the **most important officer** under the Constitution.
Union accounts are now compiled under the **Ministry of Finance**, not by the CAG.

55.s: Which of the following pairs relating to the CAG is wrongly matched?
o: Audit report on Union accounts – Submitted to the President
Audit report on State accounts – Submitted to the President
Form of accounts of the Union and States – Prescribed by the President on the CAG's advice
Appointment of the CAG – By warrant under the President's hand and seal
55.x: The audit report on State accounts is submitted to the Governor, not the President (Article 151).
n: Under Article 149, the Comptroller and Auditor General audits the receipts, expenditures, stores and accounts of the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: Oath before the President, form in the **Third Schedule**.
Salary equals an **SC judge**; fixed by **Parliament** (**Second Schedule**).
**Leave** is granted by the **President**.

55.s: What role does the CAG play once his audit reports reach the Public Accounts Committee?
o: He assists the Committee in examining them
He presents the Committee's report to the Speaker
55.x: Audit reports go first to the President or Governor and then to the legislature; the CAG then helps the PAC examine them.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General assists the Public Accounts Committee in the line-by-line examination of audit reports. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not submit audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General submits reports first to the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The claim that the Comptroller and Auditor General submits audit reports directly to the Public Accounts Committee is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General does not submit audit reports directly to Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]

55.s: What is the official name of the office of the CAG in the Constitution?
55.x: The official name is Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. “Controller” and “Attorney” are not substitutes for the constitutional terms.
xs: The official name is **Comptroller and Auditor-General of India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Not "**Controller**", not "**Attorney**", not "Accounts-General".
xa: Yet he is only an **Auditor-General**, not a true Comptroller — he has **no control over the issue of money**.
Called the "**Guardian of the public purse**".
First CAG: **V. Narahari Rao** (**1948**).

55.s: Who is described as the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the Public Accounts Committee?
55.x: The CAG assists the PAC and is called its 'friend, philosopher and guide'.
n: Union audit reports are submitted to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
State audit reports are submitted to the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General acts as the Friend, Philosopher and Guide of the Public Accounts Committee. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking action on the findings in Union audit reports rests with Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The ultimate constitutional responsibility for taking action on the findings in State audit reports rests with the State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: **PAC (2026-27):** **22 members** (**15 LS + 7 RS**); chair from the **Opposition since 1967**.
PAC was set up in **1921**.

55.s: Who described the CAG as the most important officer under the Constitution of India?
55.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution.
n: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Comptroller and Auditor General as the most important officer under the Constitution of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Comptroller and Auditor General is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Supreme Court is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Union Public Service Commission is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The Election Commission of India is one of the four bulwarks of the democratic system. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]

55.s: Which of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: Office of the CAG auditing both Union and State accounts
55.x: A single CAG audits the accounts of both the Union and the States, which is a unitary feature; the others are federal features.

55.s: Along with the Supreme Court and the Election Commission, which of the following bodies is counted with the CAG among the four bulwarks of democracy?
55.x: The CAG, Supreme Court, UPSC and Election Commission are called the four bulwarks of democracy.

55.s: What is the retirement age of a High Court judge in India?
55.x: High Court judges retire at 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment, 1963).

55.s: The retirement age of Supreme Court judges in India is
55.x: Supreme Court judges retire at 65 (Art. 124(2)); High Court judges at 62.

55.s: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India, holds the office for a duration of six years or _____ years of age (whichever comes earlier).
55.x: The CAG holds office for 6 years or till 65, whichever is earlier.

55.s: Who among the following is appointed by the President:
55.x: The President appoints the Attorney General (Art. 76), the CAG (Art. 148) and State Governors (Art. 155).

55.s: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India can be removed from his office in like manner as
o: Chairman of Union Public Service Commission
55.x: The CAG is removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge (Art. 148(1) with Art. 124(4)).

55.s: The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed by the President. He can be removed –
o: On an address from both Houses of Parliament
On the recommendation of the President by the
55.x: The CAG is removed by the President on an address by both Houses of Parliament, like a Supreme Court judge.

55.s: Which of the following is not true about the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
o: He is appointed by the President
His salary is equal to that of the Judge of Supreme
He is disqualified for any further Government office
He can be removed by the President
55.x: The CAG cannot be removed by the President on his own, only on an address of both Houses; appointment by the President, SC-judge salary and the post-retirement bar are all true.

55.s: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is appointed by-
55.x: The President appoints the CAG (Art. 148(1)).

55.s: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is the Comptroller and Auditor General of India appointed?
55.x: Article 148 provides for the CAG's appointment; Article 149 covers duties and powers.

55.s: In which Schedule is the form of the oath of office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India prescribed?
55.x: The CAG takes the oath before the President, in the form prescribed in the Third Schedule.
55.tq: Separate the Schedule dealing with oath from the Schedule dealing with salary and service conditions.
xs: The CAG takes the oath before the **President** in the form in the **Third Schedule** — option **(3)**.
⚠ The **Second Schedule** holds his **salary**, not the oath.
xa: Appointed by the **President** by **warrant under his hand and seal** (**Art. 148**).
Resigns to the **President**.
Term: **6 years or age 65**.

55.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India?
o: He holds office for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier
After ceasing to hold office, he is not eligible for further office under the Union or any State
He is removed in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge
He holds office during the pleasure of the President
55.x: The CAG does not hold office at the President's pleasure; he can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge.
xa: Removal: address by both Houses with **special majority** for proved **misbehaviour or incapacity**.
Resignation: to the **President**.
Salary **equal to an SC judge**.

55.s: On what ground can the CAG be removed on an address by both Houses of Parliament passed by special majority?
o: An adverse report of the Public Accounts Committee
55.x: Like a Supreme Court judge, the CAG is removed for proved misbehaviour or incapacity on an address by both Houses passed by special majority.
n: The Comptroller and Auditor General is removed on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General requires an address by both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The removal address must be passed by a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Proved misbehaviour or incapacity is required for removal of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: Tenure: **six years** or **65 years**, whichever is earlier.

55.s: Which Constitutional Amendment raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62 years?
55.x: The 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963 raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The retirement age of High Court Judges was raised from 60 to 62 years by the 15th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xa: **SPSC** members: **6 years or 62**.

55.s: The Chairman and members of a State Public Service Commission hold office for six years or until which age?
55.x: State PSC members serve six years or until 62, whichever is earlier; UPSC members serve six years or until 65.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge has no fixed tenure in years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires upon turning 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chairman and Members of the UPSC have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The UPSC Chairman and Members retire at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chairman and Members of an SPSC have a tenure of 6 years or until 62 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The SPSC Chairman and Members retire at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xa: HC age raised from **60 to 62** by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
The **CAG** also has **6 years or 65**.

55.s:
Assertion (A): A Supreme Court Judge has a fixed tenure of six years.
Reason (R): A Supreme Court Judge retires strictly on attaining 65 years of age under Article 124(2).
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
55.x: A is false: a Supreme Court judge has no fixed term in years. R is true: they retire at 65 under Article 124(2).
55.tq: Discriminate a retirement age from a fixed term.
n: A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 124(2) governs the retirement age of a Supreme Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge has no fixed tenure in years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires upon turning 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
xs: **A is false, but R is true** — option **(4)**.
A is wrong: a **Supreme Court Judge** has **no fixed tenure** in years.
R: SC judges retire on turning **65** (**Article 124(2)**).
xa: **CAG** and **UPSC**: **6 years or 65**, whichever earlier.
**CEC/ECs**: **6 years or 65** under the **Election Commission Act, 1991/2023**.
President / Vice-President: **5 years**.

55.s: Which of the following retires at the age of 62 years?
55.x: High Court judges and State PSC members retire at 62; Supreme Court judges, UPSC members, the CAG and Election Commissioners are in the 65 group.
n: A High Court Judge retires at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
A Supreme Court Judge retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The UPSC Chairman and Members retire at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The SPSC Chairman and Members retire at 62 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Comptroller and Auditor General retires at 65 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]

55.s: Besides Article 148(3), which law governs the tenure and retirement of the CAG?
o: CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971
55.x: The CAG's tenure comes from Article 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971; the Election Commission Act governs the Election Commissioners.
n: The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners have a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The tenure and retirement condition of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners is statutory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Election Commission condition is governed by the Election Commission Act, 1991/2023. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
The Comptroller and Auditor General has a tenure of 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]
Article 148(3) and the CAG Act, 1971 govern the tenure and retirement condition of the Comptroller and Auditor General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #78 · pp 212-215]

55.s: The removal of the CAG is governed by Article 148(1) read with which Article?
55.x: Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4) applies the Supreme Court judge's removal process to the CAG.
n: The President of India removes the Comptroller and Auditor General through the parliamentary removal process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The removal mechanism of the Comptroller and Auditor General is governed by Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: Address must pass by **special majority** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
The CAG does **not** hold office at the President's pleasure.

55.s: Which of the following is correct about the qualifications of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
o: The same as those of a Supreme Court judge
55.x: The Constitution sets no qualifications for the CAG.

55.s: To whom does the Comptroller and Auditor General of India address his resignation?
55.x: The CAG is appointed by the President and resigns to the President.

55.s: Which of the following offices has the same term of office as the CAG, that is, six years or till the age of 65?
o: Member of a State Public Service Commission
55.x: The CAG and the CEC both hold office for six years or till 65; an SPSC member retires at 62 and the President has five years.

55.s:
Which of the following provisions ensure the independence of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India ?

A. He holds office only during the pleasure of the President.

B. His salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

C. His service conditions cannot be changed to his disadvantage during his tenure.

D. He has complete control over his administrative staff.
55.src: AP Grama Ward Sachivalayam Ward Education & Data Processing
55.x: B and C are safeguards (expenses charged on the CFI; service conditions not varied to his disadvantage) and D reflects the President fixing IA&AD staff conditions only after consulting the CAG; A is wrong – he does not hold office at the President's pleasure.

55.s: Where are the salary and service conditions of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India specified?
o: First Schedule of the Constitution of India
Second Schedule of the Constitution of India
Third Schedule of the Constitution of India
Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of India
55.x: The CAG's salary and service conditions are in the Second Schedule (Part E).

55.s: How are the administrative expenses of the CAG, including the salaries and pensions of his staff, met?
o: Voted annually by the Lok Sabha
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Met from the Contingency Fund of India
Voted by both Houses of Parliament
55.x: The CAG's administrative expenses, including salaries, allowances and pensions of him and his staff, are charged on the Consolidated Fund and so are non-votable.
n: The administrative expenses of the Comptroller and Auditor General are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The charged administrative expenses are governed by Article 148(6). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The salaries of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The allowances of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
The pensions of the Comptroller and Auditor General and staff are charged expenses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Charged expenses are non-votable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]

55.s: The salary and service conditions of the CAG are provided in which Schedule of the Constitution?
55.x: The CAG's salary and service conditions are provided in the Second Schedule, and they cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment.
xa: Salary **equal to an SC judge**.
Expenses **charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India** — not votable.
**No minister** represents the CAG in Parliament.

55.s: Which of the following pairs regarding post-retirement employment is correctly matched?
o: Chairman of the UPSC – Cannot take another government job after retirement
Judges – Cannot take any job after retirement
Chairman of the UPSC – Can head commissions after retirement
Judges – Barred from heading commissions after retirement
55.x: The UPSC Chairman cannot take any further government job after retirement, whereas retired judges often head commissions and tribunals.
n: The Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission cannot take another job after retirement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
Judges can head commissions after retirement. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #80 · pp 218-221]
xa: CAG tenure: **6 years or 65**; UPSC: **6 years or 65**.
SPSC: **6 years or 62**.

55.s: Which of the following is NOT a safeguard of the CAG's independence?
o: His salary is equal to that of a Supreme Court judge
He holds office during the pleasure of the President
He is barred from further office under the Government of India or any State
His expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
55.x: The CAG does not hold office at the President's pleasure; he is removed only like a Supreme Court judge.

55.s: Who grants or refuses leave to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India?
55.x: Leave of the CAG is granted or refused by the President.

55.s: Which Schedule of the Constitution is amended to incorporate the State of Telangana in the States of India?
55.src: APPSC ASO Mains General Studies & Mental Ability 2017

55.s: The Telangana government will celebrate 2020 as the year of ____ to promote its use in various sectors such as agriculture, urban transportation and healthcare.
55.src: APPSC Junior Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020

55.s: Which of the below mentioned schedules of the Constitution would undergo a change if a new State is created?
55.x: The First Schedule lists the names and territories of the States and UTs, so creating a new State amends it (the Fourth Schedule changes too, but it is not an option).

55.s: What is a 'charged expenditure'?
o: An expenditure which has been incurred already and the bills for which are pending
Expenditure on the essential aspects of administration
The expenditure that can be incurred by the President without the approval of the Parliament
The expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India for which the approval of the Parliament is not necessary according to the Constitution
55.x: Charged expenditure is expenditure on the CFI that the Constitution makes non-votable – it does not need Parliament's vote (only discussion).

55.s: Who of the following can advance money out of the Contingency Fund of India to meet unforeseen expenses?
o: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
55.x: The Contingency Fund of India is at the disposal of the President, who makes advances out of it for unforeseen expenditure pending Parliament's authorisation (Art. 267(1)).

55.s:
Assertion (A): The Duty of Comptroller and Auditor General is not merely to ensure the legality of expenditure but also its propriety.
Reason (R): He has to uphold the Constitution and the Laws of Parliament in the field of financial administration.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not a correct
55.x: The CAG's duty is to uphold the Constitution and laws of Parliament in financial administration, which is why he checks propriety as well as legality: R explains A.

55.s: Accounts of the States are controlled by the:
55.x: State accounts are kept and audited by the CAG (he still compiles State accounts), not the Governor, CM or Finance Secretary.

55.s: In which year was accounting separated from auditing and Comptroller and Auditor General's task only remained confined to auditing the Government Accounts?
55.x: The 1976 amendment of the CAG Act, 1971 (in force 1 March 1976) separated accounts from audit.

55.s: The Amendment to (CAG Duties, Power and Condition of Service Act) 1971 separates Accounts from Audit and relieves the CAG of his responsibility in the matters of preparation of Accounts. The amendments were made in the year.
55.x: The amendment that separated accounts from audit came in 1976.

55.s: Consider the following statements: (i) It shall be the duty of the Comptroller and Auditor- General to audit all receipts which are payable into the Consolidated Fund of India. (ii) The Comptroller and Auditor General shall have authority to audit and report on the accounts of stores or stock kept in any office or department of the Union or a State. Choose the correct statement.
55.x: The CAG audits receipts payable into the CFI and the accounts of stores and stock in Union and State offices, so both are correct.

55.s: Which Article of the Constitution prescribes the duties of the comptroller and Auditor General of India?

7.s:
Consider the following pairs of rights-based laws and their guarantees:
1. RTE Act, 2009 — Free schooling for ages 6-18
2. RTI Act, 2005 — Information within 30 days
3. NREGA, 2005 — 100 days of work
Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
7.x: Pair 2 is correct: RTI (2005) guarantees information within 30 days. Pair 3 is correct: NREGA (2005) guaranteed 100 days of work. Pair 1 is wrong: RTE (2009) gives free schooling for ages 6-14 (Art. 21A), not 6-18. So (a) misses pair 3, and (c) and (d) wrongly include pair 1.
7.tq: RTE = 6-14 years under Art. 21A; RTI 30 days; NREGA 100 days.
xs: Pairs 2 and 3 are correct — option **(2)**, **2 and 3 only**.
**RTI Act, 2005** → information within **30 days**; **NREGA, 2005** → **100 days** of work.
Pair 1 is wrong: **RTE Act, 2009** gives free schooling for ages **6-14** (**Art. 21A**), not 6-18.
xa: These are **enabling** social laws; **NFSA 2013** is another.
**Protective**: Factories Act **1948**, Bonded Labour Act **1976**; **regulatory**: Minimum Wages Act **1948**, Dowry Prohibition Act **1961**.
Under the **VB-G RAM G Bill 2025**, the work guarantee is **125** days.
Social legislation marks a shift from "**freedom of contract**" to "**fairness in contract**".

xa: Development is **long-term, production-oriented**.

62.s: In August 2022 Supreme Court declared that Section 3(2) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988 as unconstitutional. Section 3(2) of this act gives provision of the following punishment.

62.s: Before the CBI can investigate a case within a State's territory, it needs the consent of that State government under which provision?

62.s:

62.s: Who can be a whistleblower under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014?
